analysis.one_liner: Blocks generic drug makers from using a fast patent-review process to challenge brand-name drug patents.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have protected brand-name drug patents from a cheap patent-challenge process, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Generic drug companies often challenge weak brand-name drug patents through a fast, low-cost Patent Office process called inter partes review, which can get cheaper generic versions to patients sooner. This bill would have forced generic and biosimilar applicants to certify that they had not filed and would not file such challenges as part of their FDA applications, and would have redefined securities fraud to cover filing such a challenge while short-selling the patent owner's stock. It would have made the most effective tool for clearing away weak drug patents much harder to use.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, whose patents would be far harder to invalidate through the Patent Office review process. Every extra month a weak patent blocks a generic competitor keeps sales at brand-name prices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require generic, brand (505(b)(2)), and biosimilar applicants to certify in their FDA filings that neither they nor any affiliated party has filed, or will file, an inter partes review or post-grant review petition against the patents they are challenging [S3].

It would also amend the Securities Exchange Act to make it a manipulative or deceptive device — the core of securities fraud — to file an inter partes review petition while making a short sale in the patent owner's stock during a 270-day window around the filing [S3].

The stated purpose is to prevent the inter partes review process from 'diminishing competition in the pharmaceutical industry' — in practice, shielding brand-name patents from the review process that generic makers have used to invalidate them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients and employers paying for prescription drugs, who would wait longer for cheaper generic and biosimilar competition when weak brand patents survive challenges. Generic drug makers would also lose their most effective route to clearing those patents.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug buyers and generic drug makers

drawbacks.text: Inter partes review is the fastest and cheapest way to invalidate a weak patent; a rule that forbids generic applicants from using it as part of FDA approval would keep weak brand patents in force longer, delaying lower-cost alternatives [S3].

The short-selling provision would treat a lawful patent challenge combined with a lawful short sale as securities fraud, chilling legitimate patent disputes and creating a novel overlap between patent law and securities law that courts and regulators would have to untangle [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to brand-name drug companies, whose patents would be harder to knock out. The costs fall on anyone who buys prescription drugs: the review process this bill restricts is one of the main ways weak drug patents get invalidated and cheaper generics reach the market. The short-selling provision adds a securities-fraud enforcement tool that would mostly deter challenges rather than help anyone. The bill's name invokes the Hatch-Waxman framework, but its effect would be to weaken the generic-competition side of that framework.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, never got a cosponsor, hearing, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Flores introduced the bill on February 6, 2019 [S5].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Financial Services Committee [S5].
No action followed the referral — no markup, no hearing, no vote — and no member signed on as a cosponsor [S4][S5].
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Generic drug makers kept their ability to challenge weak brand patents through inter partes review, and patients kept the prospect of cheaper generics. The bill's sponsor and the brand-name industry gained nothing from its death; they simply lost an opportunity.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsor signed on, so the partisan shape was never tested; the lone sponsor was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would make brand patents effectively immune from inter partes review challenges filed by generic and biosimilar applicants, extending periods of market exclusivity. The industry's gain comes directly out of drug buyers' pockets as delayed generic competition.

Generic makers rely on inter partes review to invalidate weak patents that block their entry. The certification requirement and the short-selling provision would take away or chill that tool, keeping them out of markets longer.

The bill would create a new category of manipulative conduct under securities law, expanding potential fraud liability around patent challenges and short sales. The practical effect would be less patent-challenge activity, not a market for anyone.
